Louis XVI. From 1754 to 1793, he was the last Bourbon king of France. He inherited the throne at a moment of fiscal crisis and deep social discontent. His indecisiveness, the unpopularity of his queen Marie Antoinette, and his failed attempts at reform precipitated the French Revolution and his own execution by guillotine.

He ascended to the throne in 1774 at the young age of 19, inheriting a treasury emptied by his predecessor Louis XV's wars and extravagances. He faced an impossible task from the outset. France was bankrupt, and the people were restless. In 1789, desperate to address the crisis, he called the Estates-General, a national assembly meant to raise revenue and reform the state. But the Estates-General transformed into something far greater and more radical. It became the National Assembly and authored the Declaration of the Rights of Man. Louis failed to support these revolutionary reforms, and in doing so, he lost the faith of the very reformers and moderate elements who might have contained the revolution.

His credibility collapsed entirely during the Flight to Varennes in 1791, when he attempted to flee France with Marie Antoinette. The attempt failed. They were captured, brought back to Paris in humiliation, and imprisoned. From that moment, the revolution's path turned decisively toward radicalism. The monarchy was finished.

Louis was tried for treason. On January 21, 1793, he was executed by guillotine. He declared his innocence from the scaffold, maintaining his dignity to the end. His death galvanized European monarchies against the French Republic and inspired the cascade of monarchist uprisings and foreign invasion attempts that followed. His younger brother, the comte de Provence, escaped France and claimed the throne in exile as Louis XVIII, preserving the Bourbon claim even as his brother perished on the scaffold.
